strengths: The paper proposes an interesting and timely idea: using internal LLM activations rather than only next-token probabilities for population preference prediction. Framing election forecasting as a representation-aware estimation problem is potentially original and could stimulate useful work at the intersection of mechanistic interpretability and computational social science.

The empirical scope is ambitious, spanning multiple open models, base/instruction variants, six national election contexts, multiple persona attributes, prompt templates, and representative survey benchmarks. This breadth is a real strength relative to many LLM-as-survey-response studies.

The manuscript is generally well structured and includes a clear high-level description of the method, the comparison against probability-based persona prediction, and a useful discussion that acknowledges non-uniform gains, white-box access requirements, and the approximate nature of the MLP value-vector analysis.
weaknesses: The central evidential claim is not yet well supported. Many reported win rates are around or below 50%, and the paper does not provide confidence intervals, statistical tests, effect-size summaries, or clear aggregation denominators. It is therefore hard to tell whether improvements are robust or practically meaningful rather than noise over many model/country/party/attribute comparisons.

Several analyses appear vulnerable to selection or oracle effects. Figure 3 highlights gains from choosing mechanistic estimates when they outperform probability estimates, and the entropy analysis focuses on cases with positive distance differences before evaluating high-entropy filtering. This does not convincingly establish a deployable gating rule unless the threshold/model is selected on held-out countries, parties, elections, or attributes.

The probe validation is weak for the claims made. Very high F1 on a 10% holdout from the same manually collected voting-advice statements may mostly show dataset separability rather than semantically meaningful party representations. Appendix Table 3 shows many top probe/value-vector tokens are nonsensical token fragments, which directly undermines the claim that the selected vectors encode interpretable party-aligned concepts.

The conversion from arbitrary latent activation scores to normalized party/category preference distributions is under-specified and potentially fragile. Layer-wise normalization, cosine weighting, inclusion of promoting and suppressing vectors, and aggregation over parties can strongly affect the resulting distributions, but the paper gives little ablation evidence or sensitivity analysis for these choices.

The comparison to real survey data is not fully convincing. Personas are sampled to match marginal survey distributions, but joint demographic/ideological structure and survey sampling uncertainty are not clearly handled. The method may partially benefit from survey-informed persona construction, and the evaluation lacks baselines such as survey marginals, simple demographic/ideology regressions, party prior baselines, or non-mechanistic hidden-state probes.

The presentation of results is too qualitative for a main claim of improved forecasting. Figures are difficult to read, important quantities are only shown as win rates or scatterplots, and the manuscript does not provide comprehensive numeric tables of errors by model/country/party/attribute.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper says code is available on GitHub but provides no visible URL in the manuscript, and crucial details such as exact party tokens, prompt templates for all countries, probe datasets, filtering thresholds, normalization formulas, sampling procedures, and compute requirements are insufficiently specified for reliable reproduction.

The ethics/impact treatment is inadequate. Using LLMs to infer political preferences across demographic groups has clear risks related to political targeting, representational bias, survey replacement, and misuse in campaigns, yet the impact statement says no consequences need highlighting. This is a material omission for this application area.

strengths: The paper asks an interesting and timely question: whether internal model activations can provide a better signal than next-token probabilities for LLM-based preference prediction. The framing is relevant to both mechanistic interpretability and social-science uses of LLMs.
The experimental scope is ambitious, covering several model families, base/instruction variants, six national election settings, multiple persona attributes, and prompt templates.

The proposed pipeline is clearly motivated at a high level: train party probes, select aligned MLP value vectors, aggregate persona-induced activations, and compare the resulting distributions to weighted survey benchmarks.

The paper is appropriately cautious in some parts of the discussion, noting that latent activations should not be interpreted as model beliefs and that mechanistic forecasting should complement, not replace, surveys.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence does not support the strength of the main claims. Figure 2 and Figure 4 show many win rates below or near 50%, yet the text repeatedly claims that mechanistic forecasting improves predictions across models, countries, and attributes. This makes the central contribution look selective and overstated rather than robust.

The evaluation design is weak and potentially circular. The method is evaluated mainly by relative wins against output probabilities, without strong baselines such as simpler hidden-state probes, representation classifiers trained directly for parties, random or frequency-matched value-vector selections, layer/neuron ablations, shuffled persona attributes, calibration baselines, or survey-only demographic baselines. As a result, it is unclear whether the proposed MLP value-vector mechanism is doing meaningful causal work.

The mechanistic interpretation is not convincing. The method relies on first-order MLP decomposition while abstracting away layer normalization, residual composition, and downstream interactions, but the paper then draws fairly strong conclusions about party-aligned latent representations. Table 3 is especially concerning: many top probe/value-vector tokens are garbled, multilingual fragments, or unrelated tokens, which weakens the claim that the selected vectors encode coherent party concepts.

The probe validation is insufficient. Reporting F1 above 96% on a 10% holdout from manually collected party-position statements does not demonstrate that the probes identify general party representations in persona prompts; it may simply reflect lexical/domain cues in party manifesto or voting-advice text. The paper needs out-of-domain probe validation and controls for party-name/token leakage.

The entropy-gating analysis appears post hoc and biased toward positive results. The text says the regression focuses on cases with positive distance difference and then evaluates attributes above a selected entropy threshold. This does not establish a reliable decision rule for when to use mechanistic forecasting; it risks conditioning on success and then presenting the filtered subset as evidence of consistent gains.

Reproducibility is limited. Important details are missing or under-specified, including exact probe datasets and labels, train/test splits, prompt template construction, all hyperparameters, model-access details, activation normalization, number of selected vectors per layer/party, random seeds, compute cost, and full numerical result tables with uncertainty. The paper says code is available, but the manuscript itself is not sufficient for independent reproduction or audit.

The paper lacks statistical uncertainty. Results are largely plotted as win rates or point clouds without confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, bootstrap intervals over personas/prompts/survey samples, or per-country/per-party numeric tables. Given the small number of countries and attributes, this is a major evidential gap.

The social and ethical discussion is inadequate for a paper about forecasting elections and replacing or supplementing survey measurement with LLMs. The Impact Statement says there are no societal consequences that need highlighting, which is not credible. Risks around political manipulation, demographic misrepresentation, privacy/consent in survey and web-derived model data, misuse for targeting, and harms to underrepresented groups should be discussed directly.

Presentation is sometimes unclear or internally inconsistent. The paper claims over 24 million configurations, but the method section describes 280,000 persona combinations; the relationship between these quantities is not explained clearly. Several equations and distribution definitions are hard to map onto the plotted results, and key results are not tabulated.

strengths: The paper proposes a genuinely interesting reframing of LLM-based preference prediction: instead of only aggregating next-token probabilities from persona prompts, it identifies party-aligned MLP value vectors and aggregates their persona-induced activations. This is a novel and potentially useful bridge between mechanistic interpretability and social-science forecasting.

The empirical scope is substantial: 7 open-weight models, 6 national election contexts, multiple persona attributes, prompt variations, and weighted representative survey benchmarks. This breadth makes the observed heterogeneity across countries, attributes, and model families more informative than a narrow proof of concept would be.

The method is described with reasonable mathematical clarity, including the MLP value-vector decomposition, probe training, sign-inversion validation, activation aggregation, and distributional comparison protocol. The paper also makes a sensible distinction between nominal and ordinal attributes via JS and Wasserstein distances.

The main empirical finding is useful and nuanced: latent activations often improve over output probabilities, especially for demographic/high-entropy attributes, but the gains are selective rather than universal. This avoids overclaiming a blanket replacement for probability-based estimation.

The limitations discussion is more responsible than typical for this area: the authors explicitly state that LLMs do not hold preferences, that surveys remain essential, and that the method requires white-box model access and relies on a first-order approximation.
weaknesses: The central evidence is not yet fully convincing at the level expected for a strong accept. Many reported win rates appear only modest, often around or slightly above 50%, and the paper emphasizes wins more than effect sizes, confidence intervals, or statistical significance. It is therefore difficult to assess how robust or practically meaningful the improvements are.

The construct validity of the identified value vectors is somewhat shaky. The appendix shows many top probe/vector tokens for Qwen3-14B that are garbled, unrelated, or tokenizer artifacts, with only some clearly semantically meaningful cases. This weakens the claim that the selected vectors consistently encode party concepts rather than exploiting brittle lexical or tokenization correlations.

The entropy-gating result appears post hoc and potentially circular: the analysis focuses on cases with positive distance differences and then reports improvements under a selected entropy threshold. A held-out validation of the gating rule, or a pre-registered threshold applied across all cases, would make this practical recommendation much stronger.

The probe construction and validation need more detail for reproducibility and soundness. The paper states that party-position data were manually collected and harmonized, but does not provide enough information about sample sizes, label balance, train/test splits by statement/source, possible leakage across semantically similar items, or robustness to alternate probe datasets.

The evaluation compares latent and probability estimators against survey distributions, but does not include several important baselines such as simple demographic priors, calibrated/logistic models over persona attributes, hidden-state probes not tied to MLP value vectors, or combinations learned on held-out countries/parties. These would clarify whether the mechanistic component is essential.

The causal/mechanistic interpretation remains limited. Sign-inversion validation is a useful sanity check, but the analysis still largely demonstrates correlation between selected internal activations and party-token likelihood/survey fit, not a strong mechanistic account of how preference information is represented and used across layers.

Presentation of results could be more quantitative. Figures are informative, but the paper should report aggregate tables with mean/median distance reductions, uncertainty estimates across prompts/personas/models, and explicit per-country/per-model summaries. Some claims, such as instruction tuning shifting estimates away from survey predictions, need clearer numerical support.

Ethical risks are acknowledged only briefly. Because the work targets political preference prediction from synthetic personas, the paper should more directly discuss misuse risks, demographic stereotyping, privacy-adjacent inference, and safeguards for applying such methods in political or commercial settings.

strengths: The paper proposes an original and interesting direction: using internal MLP value-vector activations, rather than only output probabilities, for population-level preference prediction. The connection between mechanistic interpretability and social-science forecasting is novel and potentially useful.

The empirical scope is ambitious, covering multiple open-weight model families, base and instruction-tuned variants, six national election settings, several persona attributes, prompt paraphrases, and representative survey benchmarks.

The methodology is described in a reasonably structured way, with probe training, value-vector selection, activation aggregation, and distributional comparison separated clearly. The paper also includes relevant controls such as shuffled-label/random-vector baselines, an in-context-learning baseline, layer-window ablations, and a non-political intervention test.

The paper acknowledges important limitations and risks, including the need for white-box access, computational cost, approximation errors in attributing MLP contributions, and potential misuse for population profiling or political micro-targeting.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is overstated relative to the presented evidence. The main win-rate figures often appear near or below 50% for many model-country-attribute combinations, yet the text repeatedly claims broad improvement. The paper needs clearer aggregate statistics, confidence intervals, and tests showing that gains are reliable rather than selective.

Several analyses appear vulnerable to ex post selection. Figure 3 highlights cases where mechanistic forecasting helps, but this is essentially an oracle comparison unless there is a pre-specified deployable rule. The entropy-gating analysis also focuses on cases with positive distance differences and uses a threshold whose selection and validation are not convincingly separated from evaluation.

The evaluation does not sufficiently establish practical forecasting value. The paper mostly compares against next-token party-probability baselines, but does not include stronger survey-modeling or social-science baselines such as multinomial/logistic models fit to available covariates, poststratification baselines, or simpler embeddings/probe-based alternatives. As a result, it is unclear whether the method is useful beyond beating a fragile LLM prompting baseline.

The mechanistic interpretation is only partially supported. Probe F1 on party-position prompts shows that parties are linearly separable from issue-position text, but this does not prove that the selected value vectors encode voter preferences in persona prompts. The top-token table contains many uninterpretable or corrupted-looking tokens, which weakens the claim that the selected vectors are semantically meaningful party directions.

The probe validation may involve leakage or insufficient independence: prompt variants and party-position examples may share statements/comments across train/test splits, and the paper does not make clear whether held-out evaluation is by distinct political items, prompt paraphrases, country, or merely random examples. Very high F1 scores are therefore hard to interpret.

Important implementation details are underspecified. The paper does not fully clarify how multi-token party names are handled, exactly how activations are normalized and converted into valid distributions, whether normalization uses information across the full evaluation set, how survey weights interact with persona sampling, or how uncertainty from finite survey samples and Monte Carlo sampling is propagated.

The work has nontrivial reproducibility barriers despite the stated code release: it depends on manually harmonized voting-advice datasets, native-speaker prompt verification, large-scale inference over many configurations, and potentially restricted survey datasets. The manuscript should provide more concrete reproducibility details and compute requirements.

The ethics discussion identifies relevant political misuse risks, but the method is explicitly aimed at extracting latent political-preference signals from models; stronger safeguards, intended-use constraints, and discussion of whether such forecasting should be performed at all in sensitive political contexts would be appropriate.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: whether LLM internals can improve preference prediction beyond surface-level persona prompting, using election forecasting as a concrete testbed.
The empirical scope is ambitious, covering multiple model families, countries, election surveys, persona attributes, prompt variants, and both base and instruction-tuned models.

The manuscript gives a reasonably clear high-level pipeline and includes several useful sanity checks, including shuffled-label/random-probe controls, sign-inversion filtering, random-vector intervention controls, and an ICL baseline using the same party-position data.

The limitations and impact statement acknowledge important concerns, including white-box access requirements, approximation limits of the MLP decomposition, survey non-substitutability, and risks of political profiling or micro-targeting.
weaknesses: The central evidential claim is not convincingly supported. The probes are trained on external party-position/voting-advice data, so it is unclear whether the method extracts latent model knowledge about human preferences or injects election-specific party-manifesto information through supervised probing. The ICL baseline helps but does not fully isolate this confound.

The evaluation protocol is underspecified and potentially fragile. The construction and normalization of attribute-level distributions are unclear, the paper alternates between P(party|category) and P(category|party), and it is not clear whether persona sampling matches joint survey distributions or only marginals. These choices can materially affect the reported distances.

The main results rely heavily on win-rates and qualitative figure interpretation rather than complete numerical results, confidence intervals, statistical tests for forecast improvements, or effect sizes. A method can win often while improving only trivially or losing badly in important cases; Figure 11 is not enough to resolve this.

The entropy gating analysis appears post hoc and partly circular: it focuses on cases with positive distance difference and selects a threshold without a held-out validation protocol. This weakens the claim that entropy is a practical decision rule for choosing mechanistic forecasting.

The baselines are insufficient for the forecasting claim. The paper compares mainly against next-token probabilities and an ICL prompt baseline, but lacks strong social-science or ML baselines such as weighted survey marginals, demographic/issue regression, calibrated direct prompting, prompt-ensemble self-consistency, tokenization-normalized party scoring, or simple models using the same persona attributes.

The mechanistic interpretation is overstated. High probe F1 on party-position statements shows that party identity is linearly recoverable from those inputs, not that selected value vectors encode human preference mechanisms. The top-token table is often dominated by uninterpretable or corrupted-looking tokens, which undermines the claimed semantic alignment.

The intervention evidence establishes that selected vectors can affect party-token logits, but not that persona-induced activations causally mediate accurate preference predictions. The bridge from token-logit manipulability to population-level survey accuracy remains weak.

Presentation has several ambiguities and inconsistencies: the paper claims over 24 million configurations but later describes 280,000 persona combinations; notation around Ψ_k and category/party distributions is hard to follow; and some prompts/tables contain apparent template or translation artifacts.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The paper says code and prompt templates are released, but the manuscript itself lacks enough detail about data harmonization, party-token scoring, random seeds for the main forecasting runs, exact normalization, sample sizes per country/category, and whether all external voting-advice datasets can be redistributed.

The ethics discussion identifies political misuse risks but gives little operational guidance on access control, deployment boundaries, or safeguards for a method explicitly designed to infer population political preferences from model internals.

strengths: The paper proposes an interesting and timely reframing of LLM-based preference prediction: instead of treating next-token probabilities as the only signal, it extracts and aggregates party-aligned internal MLP value-vector activations. This is a creative bridge between mechanistic interpretability and social-science forecasting.

The empirical scope is substantial: 7 open-weight models, base and instruction-tuned variants, 6 election contexts, multiple persona attributes, 10 prompt variants, and large-scale Monte Carlo aggregation. This breadth makes the central observation more credible than a narrow case study would.

The authors include several useful validation analyses for the latent probes, including shuffled-label and random-weight controls, regression baselines, layer-window ablations, sign-inversion filtering, non-political intervention tests, and an ICL baseline using the same party-position information. These strengthen the claim that the selected directions capture party-relevant structure rather than arbitrary linear artifacts.

The results are nuanced rather than overclaiming universal superiority: the paper shows heterogeneous gains by country, party, attribute type, and model, and it identifies high-entropy output regimes as a plausible diagnostic for when latent aggregation is more useful.

The limitations and impact discussion are unusually relevant for the application. The authors explicitly state that LLMs should not replace representative surveys, note white-box and computational constraints, discuss approximation limits in the mechanistic analysis, and acknowledge risks such as population profiling and political micro-targeting.
weaknesses: The evaluation sometimes reads as partially oracle-like. Figure 3 highlights gains from choosing mechanistic estimates when they outperform probability estimates, and the entropy analysis appears to focus on cases with positive distance difference before proposing a gating criterion. It is not clear that the gating rule is selected and evaluated on disjoint data, which weakens the practical claim that users can know when to prefer mechanistic forecasting without survey ground truth.

The mechanistic interpretation is suggestive but not fully established. The approach relies on first-order MLP value-vector decompositions, cosine alignment to binary probes, IQR-based selection, and sign-inversion tests, but these do not rule out distributed confounds or downstream residual interactions. The top-token table is often uninterpretable or corrupted-looking, which undercuts the semantic clarity of some selected vectors.

The probability-based baselines may be too limited. The main comparator is next-token probabilities over party tokens, while stronger practical alternatives such as calibrated prompting, generated-response aggregation, likelihood normalization over full party names, prompt ensembling variants, or supervised/held-out calibration are not fully explored. The ICL baseline is helpful but does not fully settle this issue.

Several design choices appear tuned on the same broad experimental suite used for reporting results, including the layer window, IQR threshold, sign-inversion gating, and entropy threshold. More explicit train/validation/test separation across countries, parties, attributes, or elections would make the evidence more convincing.

The construction of personas and comparison to survey distributions needs more detail for causal and statistical validity. Matching marginal attribute distributions may not preserve realistic joint demographic correlations, and it is unclear how survey uncertainty, party mapping differences, abstention/nonresponse, and small subgroup sample sizes affect the reported distance metrics.

Reproducibility is promising but not complete from the manuscript alone. The paper says code and configuration files are released, but many crucial ingredients depend on manual harmonization of party-position data, native-speaker verification, prompt variants, and survey preprocessing; these need enough detail and artifacts for independent reconstruction.

The contribution is important and original, but the empirical gains are heterogeneous and often modest in win-rate terms, with some countries/models below or near 50%. This supports a weak accept more than a full accept unless the authors clarify the non-oracle gating and strengthen the baselines.
